title: Spirituals and Work Songs
objective: After this level you can describe the songs of enslaved African Americans and their legacy.
summary: Enslaved African Americans created spirituals, passed on only by live singing and built on call-and-response. Work songs kept crews in rhythm; out of both came the blues.

cards.headline: The songs that carried a people through slavery were never written down.
cards.body: Enslaved African Americans made their songs without paper, passing them on by voice alone. Yet those songs lasted, and out of them, in time, came the blues. How did music with no sheet music survive, and what was it really saying?

cards.headline: Spirituals: passed voice to voice, leader to chorus
cards.body: The Library of Congress describes spirituals as religious folk songs created and sung by enslaved people of African descent in the American South. Through the whole era of slavery, they passed from one generation to the next only by live singing. Their shape helped: a leader sings a line and the chorus answers with a refrain, often over clapping and patting. That's call-and-response, and a song built that way is easy to join and hard to forget.

mascot.line: Keep this shape: a leader's line, a group's answer. You'll hear it all chapter.

cards.headline: A Bible story with a second meaning
cards.body: "Go Down, Moses" retells the Exodus: Moses tells Pharaoh to free the Israelites from slavery in Egypt, and the congregation answers, "Let my people go!" On the surface, it's scripture. But it was sung by enslaved people, about enslaved people demanding freedom from a far more powerful master. Music scholars hear in it a direct expression of their longing for freedom.

cards.headline: Work songs: music that keeps a crew in step
cards.body: Work songs had a different job. Singing passed the time and kept a crew moving together, and many crews had a leader who sang a line while the others answered with a refrain. Sound familiar? Britannica traces a long thread from here: during and after slavery, Black American workers built spirituals and, ultimately, the blues out of older work song traditions. Keep hold of that thread; the next level pulls it.

cards.fact: In 1873, a student choir sang spirituals for Queen Victoria, and its tour paid for a college building.
cards.context: Fisk University, founded in 1865 to educate formerly enslaved people, was deep in debt by 1871, so a professor formed a student choir to raise money. The Fisk Jubilee Singers carried spirituals, rarely heard outside Black churches and homes, to audiences in the US and Europe. Tour proceeds built Fisk's Jubilee Hall.

questions.prompt: According to the Library of Congress, how were spirituals passed down during slavery?

options.label: In printed hymnals sold in the South
options.rationale: They passed on without paper, by voice.

options.label: Through live singing, generation to generation
On early phonograph recordings
options.rationale: Spirituals were passed on by live singing throughout slavery.

options.label: Through lessons at music schools
options.rationale: They were passed on by people singing them.

questions.explanation: Throughout slavery, spirituals were passed from one generation to the next only by live, oral transmission.

questions.prompt: Why did the spiritual "Go Down, Moses" carry special meaning for enslaved singers?

options.label: It was a dance song for celebrations
options.rationale: It's a religious song retelling the Exodus.

options.label: It was written by a famous European composer
options.rationale: It came from enslaved communities in the American South.

options.label: It told of enslaved people demanding freedom
It was about farming and the seasons

questions.explanation: The Exodus story of Israelites freed from slavery, with its answer "Let my people go!", voiced enslaved people's longing for freedom.
